label: thm:full-dimension
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:full-dimension}
Let \(A,B\subset\mathbb R^2\) be nonempty Borel sets. Then for almost all
\(g\in\mathrm O(2)\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-dimension}
 \dim_{\mathrm H}(gA-B)\ge\min\{\dim_{\mathrm H} A+\dim_{\mathrm H} B,2\}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, let \(\mu,\nu\) be compactly supported probability measures
with Frostman exponents \(\alpha,\beta\in(0,2]\), respectively. There
is a Borel set \(\mathcal G\subset\mathrm O(2)\) with \(m(\mathcal G)=1\) such that, for every
\(g\in\mathcal G\) and every Borel set \(S\subset\mathbb R^2\),
\[
 \dim_{\mathrm H} S<\min\{\alpha+\beta,2\}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 ((g_\#\mu)*\widetilde\nu)(S)=0.
\]
Here \(\widetilde\nu(E)=\nu(-E)\).
head: environment

label: thm:breaking-four-thirds
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:breaking-four-thirds}
Let \(t>s_0\), and let \(\mu,\nu\) be compactly supported
\(t\)-Frostman probability measures on \(\mathbb R^2\). Then for almost all
\(g\in\mathrm O(2)\),
\[
 (g_\#\mu)*\widetilde\nu\ll\mathcal L^2.
\]
In particular, if \(A,B\subset\mathbb R^2\) are Borel sets with
\(\min\{\dim_{\mathrm H} A,\dim_{\mathrm H} B\}>s_0\), then
\(\mathcal L^2(gA-B)>0\) for almost all \(g\in\mathrm O(2)\).

label: fd:lem:cover
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{fd:lem:cover}
Let \(d>0\), let \(K\subset\mathbb R^2\) be bounded and let \(S\subset K\) with
\(\dim_{\mathrm H} S<d\). For every integer \(j_{0}\ge1\), there is a countable
family $\mathcal Q$ of dyadic squares meeting $K$ such that
\[
 S\subset\bigcup_{Q\in\mathcal Q}Q,\qquad
 \operatorname{side}(Q)\le2^{-j_{0}},\qquad
 \sum_{Q\in\mathcal Q}\operatorname{side}(Q)^d\le1.
\]
At each scale \(2^{-j}\), the family therefore contains at most
$\lfloor2^{jd}\rfloor$ squares.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\mathcal H^d(S)=0$, we may cover $S$ by balls of radii
$r_i\le2^{-j_0-1}$ with
\[
 \sum_i r_i^d\le(16\cdot2^d)^{-1}.
\]
Each ball is covered by at most $16$ dyadic squares whose side length is
between $r_i$ and $2r_i$. We discard squares that do not meet $S$ and
remove repetitions. The resulting family $\mathcal Q$ satisfies
\[
 \operatorname{side}(Q)\le2^{-j_0},\qquad
 \sum_{Q\in\mathcal Q}\operatorname{side}(Q)^d
 \le16\cdot2^d\sum_i r_i^d\le1.
\]
Thus,
\[
 |\{Q\in\mathcal Q:\operatorname{side}(Q)=2^{-j}\}|\,2^{-jd}
 \le\sum_{Q\in\mathcal Q}\operatorname{side}(Q)^d\le1.
\]
This completes the proof.

label: fd:lem:cayley
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{fd:lem:cayley}
For $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\theta=2\arctan u$,
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:cayley}
 (\operatorname{Id}-u\mathsf J)(R_\theta a-b)=p+uv.
\end{equation}
On every bounded interval of $u$, the change of coordinates
\[
 (\theta,z)\longmapsto\bigl(u,(\operatorname{Id}-u\mathsf J)z\bigr)
\]
is smooth and invertible. Both $d\theta/du$ and its spatial Jacobian
are bounded above and below by positive constants.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Cayley formula reads
\[
 R_{2\arctan u}
 =\frac{(1-u^2)\operatorname{Id}+2u\mathsf J}{1+u^2}.
\]
Since $\mathsf J^2=-\operatorname{Id}$, multiplication gives
$(\operatorname{Id}-u\mathsf J)R_{2\arctan u}=\operatorname{Id}+u\mathsf J$. Thus,
\[
 (\operatorname{Id}-u\mathsf J)(R_\theta a-b)
 =a-b+u\mathsf J(a+b)=p+uv.
\]
The remaining bounds follow from
\[
 \det(\operatorname{Id}-u\mathsf J)=1+u^2,
 \qquad \frac{d\theta}{du}=\frac{2}{1+u^2}.
\]
This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: fd:lem:localization
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{fd:lem:localization}
Suppose \(W\) has dimensions \(r_1\times r_2\times h\), where
\(0<r_1\le r_2\le8\) and \(h\le8\). Then
\(\mathcal A(W)\cap\mathcal P\) has diameter at most \(Cr_2\). In
particular, its preimage under \(\mathscr L\)
is contained in a product of two planar balls of radius $Cr_2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $r_2$ is bounded below, the diameter bound follows from the boundedness
of $\mathcal {P}$. We may therefore assume that $r_2$ is small and
$\mathcal A(W)\cap\mathcal P$ is nonempty. Let $(p,v)$ belong to this
intersection. The points of its segment with $u=-1/3$ and $u=1/3$ are
at distance at least $2/3$ from each other. Thus,
\[
 h^2+r_1^2+r_2^2\ge4/9.
\]
Since $r_2$ is small, $h$ is bounded below and is the longest side of $W$.
We call the line through the centre of $W$ parallel to that side its
longitudinal axis. The components of the difference of the two segment
points perpendicular to this axis have magnitude at most $Cr_2$. Hence, the axis makes an angle $O(r_2)$ with the segment.
Since $|v|$ is small, the $u$-component of the axis is bounded away from zero, so we can write the axis as $(u,p_0+uv_0)$.

Every point $(u,x)\in W$ is within $Cr_2$ of an axis point
$(u',p_0+u'v_0)$. Since $|v_0|$ is bounded,
\[
 |x-p_0-uv_0|
 \le |x-p_0-u'v_0|+|u'-u|\,|v_0|\le Cr_2.
\]
Applying this at $u=\pm1/3$ on each contained segment gives
\[
 |p-p_0+(v-v_0)/3|+|p-p_0-(v-v_0)/3|\le Cr_2.
\]
Adding and subtracting gives $|p-p_0|+|v-v_0|\le Cr_2$.
The preimage bound follows from \eqref{fd:eq:inverse}. This completes
the proof.
head: environment

label: fd:prop:product
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We shall evaluate the constraint from the narrowest slab of the prism
at two points of each segment. This gives two independent constraints
on each point of the pair. After fixing one point, these
constraints place the other in a ball of radius $Cr_1$.

By Lemma~\ref{fd:lem:localization}, there are planar balls $B_1,B_2$ of
radius $Cr_2$ such that
\[
 \mathscr L^{-1}(\mathcal A(W)\cap\mathcal P)\subset B_{1}\times B_{2}.
\]

Let $(n_0,n)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2$ be a unit normal to the pair of faces
separated by $r_1$. The corresponding slab can be written as
\[
 |n_0u+n\cdot x-c|\le r_1/2.
\]
Substituting $x=p+uv$ at $u=\pm1/3$ yields
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:slab-constraints}
 |n\cdot p-c|\le Cr_1,
 \qquad |n_0+n\cdot v|\le Cr_1.
\end{equation}
For sufficiently small $r_1$, the second inequality and the small bound
on $|v|$ imply \(|n|\ge c_0>0\). Otherwise \(|n_0|\) would be close
to one, contradicting that inequality.

For a fixed $a$, inserting $p=a-b$ and $v=\mathsf J(a+b)$ into
\eqref{fd:eq:slab-constraints} gives
\[
 |n\cdot a-n\cdot b-c|\le Cr_1,\qquad
 |n\cdot\mathsf Jb+(n_0+n\cdot\mathsf Ja)|\le Cr_1.
\]
The coefficient matrix is
\[
 M_n=\begin{pmatrix}-n^{\mathsf T}\\ n^{\mathsf T}\mathsf J\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its two rows are perpendicular and have norm $|n|$, so
$|\det M_n|=|n|^2\ge c_0^2$ and its inverse has uniformly bounded norm.
For this fixed $a$, all admissible $b$ therefore lie in a ball of radius
$Cr_1$. Integrating the $\beta$-Frostman estimate over the ball containing
the \(a\)-coordinates, of radius $Cr_2$, gives
\[
 \eta(\mathcal A(W))\le Cr_1^\beta r_2^\alpha.
\]
Fixing $b$ instead and using the two independent constraints on $a$
gives $Cr_1^\alpha r_2^\beta$. When $r_1$ is bounded below, both estimates
follow from total mass one after changing the constant. This proves
\eqref{fd:eq:anisotropic}.

To prove \eqref{fd:eq:prism-bound}, we may assume that $\alpha\ge\beta$,
since \eqref{fd:eq:anisotropic} is symmetric in the exponents.
Suppose first that $\alpha+\beta\le2$, so $s=\alpha+\beta$.
Let $x_1=r_1/\rho$ and $x_2=r_2/\rho$. Then $1\le x_1\le x_2$ and
\[
 \rho^{-s}r_1^\alpha r_2^\beta=x_1^\alpha x_2^\beta.
\]
If $\alpha\le1$, then $\beta\le1$ and this is at most $x_1x_2$.
If $\alpha>1$, then
\[
 \frac{x_1^\alpha x_2^\beta}{x_1x_2}
 =x_1^{\alpha-1}x_2^{\beta-1}
 \le x_2^{\alpha+\beta-2}\le1.
\]
Thus, \eqref{fd:eq:anisotropic} gives \eqref{fd:eq:prism-bound}.

If $\alpha+\beta\ge2$, then $s=2$ and $\alpha\ge1$. For
$0<r_1\le r_2\le1$,
\[
 \frac{r_1^\alpha r_2^\beta}{r_1r_2}
 =\left(\frac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^{\alpha-1}
   r_2^{\alpha+\beta-2}\le1.
\]
For $r_2\le8$, the same expression is bounded by a fixed constant.
This proves \eqref{fd:eq:prism-bound} also in this case.
The preimage of a parameter ball under $\mathscr L$ is contained in a
product of two balls of radius $Cr$. Hence, its product mass is at most
$Cr^{\alpha+\beta}\le Cr^s$ for $r\le1$, proving
\eqref{fd:eq:parameter-ball}. Every positive measure $\eta_0\le\eta$
inherits the same upper bounds. This completes the proof.

label: fd:thm:WZ
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{fd:thm:WZ}
For every $\varepsilon>0$, there exist $K_{\rm WZ}>1$ and $\rho_\varepsilon>0$
with the following property. Let $0<\rho<\rho_\varepsilon$, and let
$\mathcal T$ be a finite, essentially distinct family of $\rho$-tubes contained
in the unit ball of $\mathbb R^3$. Suppose that every rectangular prism of
dimensions $r_1\times r_2\times2$ contains at most
$100r_1r_2\rho^{-2}$ tubes of $\mathcal T$. If $0<\lambda\le1$ and
$|Y(T)|\ge\lambda|T|$ for every $T\in\mathcal T$, then
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:WZ}
 \left|\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal T}Y(T)\right|
 \ge\rho^\varepsilon\lambda^{K_{\rm WZ}}\sum_{T\in\mathcal T}|T|.
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: Wang--Zahl

label: fd:lem:selection
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{fd:lem:selection}
Suppose that \eqref{fd:eq:prism-bound} and \eqref{fd:eq:parameter-ball}
hold with $\eta_0$ in place of $\eta$, for the fixed exponent $s$
and a fixed constant. If $\delta$ is sufficiently small and
$a_G\ge\delta^{s/2}$, then there is
$\mathcal S\subset G$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:selection-size}
 |\mathcal S|\ge
 c\,\frac{a_G\rho^{-s}}{(\log(1/\rho))^4},
\end{equation}
and the tubes $\{T_i:i\in\mathcal S\}$ satisfy all the geometric
hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{fd:thm:WZ}. The constants and the upper bound
on $\delta$ may depend on $s$ and the constant in the two assumed bounds,
but are independent of $G$ and of the measure $\eta_0$ within those bounds.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first sample the tubes independently according to their weights.
The prism estimate controls the number selected in each sufficiently
large prism. We then remove tubes with nearby parameters. This gives
the required bound for smaller prisms and makes the remaining tubes
essentially distinct.

Let $L_{\rho}=\log(1/\rho)$. We select the indices in $G$ independently with
probabilities
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:probability}
 \mathbb P(i\text{ is selected})
 =\frac{w_i}{C_2\rho^sL_{\rho}^4}.
\end{equation}
The ball bound gives $w_i\le C\delta^s$, so these are valid probabilities
for $C_2$ fixed sufficiently large and $\delta$ sufficiently small.
If $X$ is the number selected, then
\[
 M_0:=\mathbb EX=\frac{a_G}{C_2\rho^sL_{\rho}^4},\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}X\le M_0.
\]
Since $a_G\ge\delta^{s/2}$ and $\rho=C_{\rm fd}\delta$,
\[
 M_0\ge c_s\delta^{-s/2}(\log(1/\delta))^{-4}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Here $s>0$ is fixed, and the convergence is uniform in $G$ and
$\eta_0$ under the stated bounds. By Chebyshev's inequality,
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:sample-lower}
 \mathbb P(X<M_0/2)\le4/M_0=o(1).
\end{equation}

We first choose a collection of at most $\rho^{-N_0}$ test prisms, for a fixed
absolute $N_0$, with the following property. Every
$r_1\times r_2\times2$ prism $W$ containing a $\rho$-tube in the unit
ball has an associated test prism $W'$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:net}
 W\cap B(0,1)\subset W',\qquad
 r'_1\le4r_1,\quad r'_2\le4r_2,
\end{equation}
where the transverse widths are ordered so that
$\rho\le r'_1\le r'_2\le4$, and the length of $W'$ is at most six.
To construct this collection, we first truncate widths exceeding two when
covering $W\cap B(0,1)$, and we replace the longitudinal constraint by an
interval of length two containing the projection of the unit ball. The
resulting centres lie in a bounded set. We then round the transverse widths
upward to dyadic values and approximate the centres and orthonormal frames
by finite nets of accuracy $\rho^3$. Finally, we double the rounded widths
and enlarge the length to six. Because the approximation error is
$O(\rho^3)$ and the relevant widths are at least $2\rho$ whenever $W$
contains a $\rho$-tube, this construction gives \eqref{fd:eq:net}. The
centre and frame nets have polynomial cardinality in $\rho^{-1}$, while the
two dyadic width choices contribute only a logarithmic factor. Thus, after
increasing $N_0$, the total cardinality is at most $\rho^{-N_0}$.

For each test prism $W'$, denote by $X_{W'}$ the number of selected tubes
contained in it. The sum of the weights $w_i$ over all indices
$i\in G$ with $T_i\subset W'$ is at most
$C\rho^{s-2}r'_1r'_2$. To see this, notice that the segments depend Lipschitz
continuously on $(p,v)$ in the bounded parameter region. Hence, all
parameters in the cubes of those representatives have their segments in
an $O(\delta)$ enlargement of $W'$. For sufficiently small $\delta$, this enlargement has transverse
widths comparable to $r'_1,r'_2$, and all its dimensions are at most eight.
The prism estimate then applies. With
$k_{W'}=r'_1r'_2\rho^{-2}$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:prism-expectation}
 \mathbb EX_{W'}\le\frac{Ck_{W'}}{C_2L_{\rho}^4}.
\end{equation}
For a sum $X_{\rm B}$ of independent Bernoulli variables with mean
$M_{\rm B}>0$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:bernoulli}
 \mathbb P(X_{\rm B}\ge k)\le(eM_{\rm B}/k)^k
\end{equation}
for $k\ge M_{\rm B}$. Independence gives
\[
 \mathbb E e^{s_{\rm B}X_{\rm B}}
 \le\exp\bigl((e^{s_{\rm B}}-1)M_{\rm B}\bigr)
 \quad\text{for }s_{\rm B}\ge0.
\]
The exponential Markov inequality with $e^{s_{\rm B}}=k/M_{\rm B}$ gives
\[
 \mathbb P(X_{\rm B}\ge k)
 \le\exp\bigl(-s_{\rm B}k+(e^{s_{\rm B}}-1)M_{\rm B}\bigr)
 \le(eM_{\rm B}/k)^{k}.
\]
The claim is immediate when $M_{\rm B}=0$.

We choose $C_{5}>N_0+10$. If $k_{W'}\ge C_{5}L_{\rho}$, then
\eqref{fd:eq:bernoulli}, applied with $k=\lceil k_{W'}\rceil$, together
with \eqref{fd:eq:prism-expectation}, shows that the failure probability
is at most $e^{-k_{W'}}$ for sufficiently small $\rho$. A union bound
over the test prisms has total failure probability at most
\[
 \rho^{-N_{0}}e^{-C_{5}L_{\rho}}=\rho^{C_{5}-N_{0}}=o(1).
\]
Thus, with probability $1-o(1)$,
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:large-counts}
 X_{W'}\le2k_{W'}
\end{equation}
for $k_{W'}\ge C_{5}L_{\rho}$.

This leaves the prisms with $k_{W'}<C_{5}L_{\rho}$. We treat them by
separating nearby parameters. Let
\[
 r_0=C_3\rho L_{\rho},
\]
where $C_3$ is large relative to $C_{5}$ and the constant in
Lemma~\ref{fd:lem:localization}. Let $N_{\rm pair}$ be the number of
unordered pairs of distinct selected indices with $|q_i-q_j|\le r_0$.
If $|q_i-q_j|\le r_0$, then $Q_j\cap\mathcal P\subset B(q_i,r_0+C\delta)$.
Thus, the parameter ball estimate gives
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E N_{\rm pair}
 &\le\frac{C}{C_2^2\rho^{2s}L_{\rho}^8}
       \sum_{i\in G}w_i
       \sum_{j:\,|q_i-q_j|\le r_0}w_j\\
 &\le\frac{C a_G r_0^s}{C_2^2\rho^{2s}L_{\rho}^8}
 \le C_s M_0L_{\rho}^{s-4}=o(M_0).
\end{align*}
Since $s\le2$, the last logarithmic power tends to zero.
By Markov's inequality, \(N_{\rm pair}\le M_0/8\) with probability \(1-o(1)\).
The preceding probability estimates allow us to choose an outcome for
which \(N_{\rm pair}\le M_0/8\), \(X\ge M_0/2\), and
\eqref{fd:eq:large-counts} all hold. From this outcome, we remove every selected index belonging to a pair at distance at most $r_0$. At most $2N_{\rm pair}\le M_0/4$ indices are removed, so at least $M_0/4$ remain. Their parameters are $r_0$-separated. If a test prism has $k_{W'}<C_{5}L_{\rho}$, then $r'_1\ge\rho$ implies $r'_2<C_{5}\rho L_{\rho}$.
Lemma~\ref{fd:lem:localization} shows that the parameters of its contained segments have diameter at most $CC_{5}\rho L_{\rho}<r_0$. Such a prism contains
at most one remaining tube.

For an arbitrary $r_1\times r_2\times2$ prism, we compare it with its
associated test prism. In the large case, the number of remaining tubes is
at most
\[
 2r'_1r'_2\rho^{-2}\le32r_1r_2\rho^{-2}
 \le100r_1r_2\rho^{-2}.
\]
In the small case it is at most one, and the same final bound holds:
a prism containing a $\rho$-tube has both transverse widths at least
$2\rho$.

It remains to prove essential distinctness. For parameters in \(\mathcal P\),
the intersection of any tube with
a time slice has area at most $C\rho^2$. If two tubes intersected in
more than half their common volume, the set of times at which their
slices meet would have length bounded below by an absolute constant.
At each such time,
\[
 |p_i-p_j+u(v_i-v_j)|\le C\rho.
\]
Here the same estimate also holds near the rounded tube ends, since a
point in a tube is within $\rho$ of an axis point, and the slopes are
bounded. We may choose two such times $u_1,u_2$ with $|u_{1}-u_{2}|\ge c>0$. Then
\[
 |u_{1}-u_{2}|\,|v_{i}-v_{j}|\le C\rho,
 \qquad |p_i-p_j|\le C\rho+|u_{1}|\,|v_i-v_j|\le C\rho.
\]
This contradicts $r_0$-separation for small
$\rho$. Thus, the remaining tubes are essentially distinct.
Their containment in the unit ball follows from \eqref{fd:eq:normalization}
and \eqref{fd:eq:segment}. Their number is at least $M_0/4$, so
\eqref{fd:eq:selection-size} follows.
This completes the proof.

label: fd:prop:testing
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{fd:prop:testing}
Let $\mu,\nu$ be compactly supported Frostman probabilities with exponents
$\alpha,\beta\in(0,2]$, and suppose that \eqref{fd:eq:normalization} holds.
Set $s=\min\{\alpha+\beta,2\}$. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there are
$Q_{\rm test}=Q_{\rm test}(\varepsilon)>2$, $C_\varepsilon<\infty$, and
$\delta_\varepsilon>0$ such that, for every measurable
$\Omega\subset I_0\times\mathbb R^2$ and $0<\delta<\delta_\varepsilon$,
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:testing}
 \int_\Omega F_\delta(u,x)\,d u\,d x
 \le C_\varepsilon\left(
        \delta^{s/2}+\bigl(\delta^{-(2-s)-\varepsilon}|\Omega|\bigr)^{1/Q_{\rm test}}\right).
\end{equation}
The exponent $Q_{\rm test}$ depends only on $\varepsilon$. The constants
and $\delta_\varepsilon$ may also depend on the fixed Frostman exponents
and constants, but are independent of $\Omega$ and $\delta$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If the left-hand side of \eqref{fd:eq:testing} is small, the first term
on the right suffices. Otherwise, a positive amount of the total weight
lies on tubes for which $\Omega$ occupies a definite proportion of the
volume. We apply Lemma~\ref{fd:lem:selection} to those tubes and use the
Wang--Zahl theorem to bound $|\Omega|$ from below.

We use the cubes $Q_i$, weights $w_i$ and tubes $T_i$ defined before
Lemma~\ref{fd:lem:selection}, taking $\eta_0=\eta$ from
\eqref{fd:eq:eta}. Proposition~\ref{fd:prop:product} verifies its hypotheses.
The support and upper bound of $\varphi$ give, on $I_0\times\mathbb R^2$,
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:domination}
 F_\delta(u,x)\le C\delta^{-2}\sum_i w_i\mathbf 1_{T_i}(u,x).
\end{equation}
For each $(p,v)\in Q_{i}$ with $\varphi_\delta(x-p-uv)\ne0$, the choice
of $C_{\rm fd}$ gives $(u,x)\in T_{i}$.

We set
\[
 a_{\Omega}=\int_\Omega F_\delta,\qquad
 d_i=\frac{|\Omega\cap T_i|}{|T_i|}\in[0,1].
\]
Since $|T_i|\asymp\delta^2$, \eqref{fd:eq:domination} gives
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:mass-richness}
 a_{\Omega}\le C_4\sum_i w_i d_i.
\end{equation}
Here we take $C_4\ge1$. If $a_{\Omega}\le2C_4\delta^{s/2}$, the first term in \eqref{fd:eq:testing} suffices.
Otherwise, let
\[
 G=\{i:d_i\ge a_{\Omega}/(2C_4)\}.
\]
Because $\sum\limits_iw_i=1$, the complementary indices contribute at most
$a_{\Omega}/(2C_4)$ to $\sum\limits_iw_id_i$. It follows that
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:good-mass}
 a_G=\sum_{i\in G}w_i
 \ge\sum_{i\in G}w_i d_i\ge a_{\Omega}/(2C_4)>\delta^{s/2}.
\end{equation}
By Lemma~\ref{fd:lem:selection}, there is $\mathcal S\subset G$ with
\eqref{fd:eq:selection-size} whose tubes satisfy the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{fd:thm:WZ}. We apply that theorem with $\varepsilon/2$ in
place of $\varepsilon$ and with $Y(T_i)=\Omega\cap T_i$. These shadings
have relative volume at least $\lambda=a_{\Omega}/(2C_4)$.
By \eqref{fd:eq:totalmass}, $0<a_{\Omega}\le|I_0|=1/2$, so
$0<\lambda\le1$. If $K_{\rm WZ}>1$ is the exponent in that theorem, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 |\Omega|
 &\ge\left|\bigcup_{i\in\mathcal S}Y(T_i)\right|\\
 &\ge\rho^{\varepsilon/2}
       \left(\frac{a_{\Omega}}{2C_4}\right)^{K_{\rm WZ}}
       \sum_{i\in\mathcal S}|T_i|\\
 &\ge c_\varepsilon\delta^{2-s+\varepsilon/2}
       a_{\Omega}^{K_{\rm WZ}}\frac{a_G}{(\log(1/\rho))^4}
 \ge c'_\varepsilon\delta^{2-s+\varepsilon}a_{\Omega}^{K_{\rm WZ}+1}.
\end{align*}
Here we used $|T_i|\asymp\rho^2$ and \eqref{fd:eq:selection-size}.
The last step uses
\eqref{fd:eq:good-mass} and the inequality
\[
 (\log(1/\rho))^{-4}\ge c_\varepsilon\delta^{\varepsilon/2},
\]
which holds for sufficiently small $\delta$.
We set $Q_{\rm test}=K_{\rm WZ}+1>2$ and solve the preceding inequality for
$a_{\Omega}$. Combining the resulting bound with the case
$a_{\Omega}\le2C_4\delta^{s/2}$ proves \eqref{fd:eq:testing}. This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: fd:rem:dimension-not-area
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{fd:rem:dimension-not-area}
The Wang--Zahl theorem is the only non-elementary input in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:full-dimension}. For fixed $\varepsilon$, the estimate
\eqref{fd:eq:testing} has a fixed positive exponent $1/Q_{\rm test}$.
A cover with at most $\delta^{-d}$ squares of side $\delta$, where $d<s$,
gives $|\Omega|\lesssim\delta^{2-d}$,
so the second term is at most $C\delta^{(s-d-\varepsilon)/Q_{\rm test}}$.
We may choose $\varepsilon<s-d$ for each fixed $d$. No uniform bound for
$Q_{\rm test}$ as $d\uparrow s$ is needed. At $s=2$, the estimate still
does not give positive Lebesgue measure.
head: environment

label: prop:full-dimension-measure
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:full-dimension-measure}
Let \(\mu,\nu\) be compactly supported Frostman probability measures on
\(\mathbb R^2\) with exponents \(\alpha,\beta\in(0,2]\), respectively. Set
\(s=\min\{\alpha+\beta,2\}\). There is a Borel set \(\mathcal G\subset\mathrm O(2)\),
with \(m(\mathrm O(2)\setminus\mathcal G)=0\), such that for every
\(g\in\mathcal G\) and every Borel set \(S\subset\mathbb R^2\) with
\(\dim_{\mathrm H} S<s\),
\[
 \lambda_g(S)=0.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For each $d<s$, we control simultaneously all unions of at most
$2^{jd}$ dyadic squares at scale $2^{-j}$. The testing estimate and
Borel--Cantelli give a null set outside which the mass of every such
union tends to zero at a summable rate. The covering lemma then gives
the conclusion for every Borel set of dimension less than $d$.

We first prove the claim in the line coordinates, assuming
\eqref{fd:eq:normalization}. All the probabilities $\lambda'_u$,
$u\in I_0$, are supported in a fixed closed bounded square $K_0\subset\mathbb R^2$.
We fix a rational number $d\in(0,s)$ and set $\delta_j=2^{-j}$. We denote
by $\mathcal D_j$ the finite family of dyadic squares of side $\delta_j$ meeting
$K_0$. We define
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:Hj}
 H_j(u)=\max\left\{
 \lambda'_u\left(\bigcup\mathcal Q\right):
 \mathcal Q\subset\mathcal D_j,\quad
 |\mathcal Q|\le\lfloor2^{jd}\rfloor\right\},
\end{equation}
and
\[
 E_j=\{u\in I_0:H_j(u)>j^{-2}\}.
\]
For each fixed Borel square $Q$, the map
\[
 u\longmapsto\lambda'_u(Q)
 =\int\mathbf 1_Q(p+uv)\,d\eta(p,v)
\]
is Borel. The same holds for a finite union of squares. Since the
maximum in \eqref{fd:eq:Hj} is over finitely many families, $H_j$ and $E_j$
are Borel.

We enumerate those finite families and, for each $u\in E_j$, denote by
$\mathcal Q_j(u)$ the first family attaining the maximum in
\eqref{fd:eq:Hj}. The parameter set on which any particular family is
chosen is Borel. We define $\Omega_j\subset I_0\times\mathbb R^2$ by its sections:
\[
 (\Omega_j)_u=
 \begin{cases}
 N_{\delta_j}\!\left(\displaystyle\bigcup\mathcal Q_j(u)\right),
       &u\in E_j,\\[2mm]
 \varnothing,&u\notin E_j.
 \end{cases}
\]
Here $N_r$ denotes the open $r$-neighbourhood in $\mathbb R^2$.
$\Omega_j$ is Borel because it is a finite union of products of Borel
parameter sets with fixed open subsets of $\mathbb R^2$. Each section is a union
of at most $2^{jd}$ enlarged squares of area at most $C\delta_j^2$. Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:Omega-size}
 |\Omega_j|\le C\delta_j^{2-d}.
\end{equation}

For \(u\in E_j\), the nonnegativity of \(\varphi_{\delta_j}\), its support
in \(B(0,\delta_j)\), and the identity
\(\int\varphi_{\delta_j}=1\) give
\[
 \int_{(\Omega_j)_u}F_{\delta_j}(u,x)\,d x
 \ge \lambda'_u\left(\bigcup\mathcal Q_j(u)\right)=H_j(u).
\]
Hence,
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:Omega-mass}
 \int_{\Omega_j}F_{\delta_j}\,d u\,d x
 \ge\int_{E_j}H_j(u)\,d u
 \ge j^{-2}\mathcal L^1(E_j).
\end{equation}

We apply Proposition~\ref{fd:prop:testing} with
$\varepsilon=(s-d)/2$ and fix the resulting exponent
$Q_{\rm test}=Q_{\rm test}((s-d)/2)$. Since
\[
 \bigl(\delta_j^{-(2-s)-\varepsilon}\delta_j^{2-d}\bigr)^{1/Q_{\rm test}}
 =\delta_j^{(s-d)/(2Q_{\rm test})},
\]
\eqref{fd:eq:Omega-size} and \eqref{fd:eq:Omega-mass} give, for all
sufficiently large $j$,
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:exceptional-sum}
 \mathcal L^1(E_j)
 \le C_{s,d}j^2\left(2^{-js/2}+2^{-j(s-d)/(2Q_{\rm test})}\right).
\end{equation}
For the fixed $s$ and $d$, both series on the right are summable.
Their constants need not be uniform as $d\uparrow s$. Borel--Cantelli
now gives a Borel null set $Z_d\subset I_0$ such that, for every
$u\in I_0\setminus Z_d$ and all sufficiently large $j$,
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:small-covers}
 H_j(u)\le j^{-2}.
\end{equation}

We now fix $u\notin Z_d$ and a Borel set $S\subset\mathbb R^2$ with $\dim_{\mathrm H} S<d$.
Since $\lambda'_u$ is supported in $K_0$, it is enough to consider $S\cap K_0$.
For each sufficiently large $j_0$, Lemma~\ref{fd:lem:cover} provides a dyadic
cover of $S\cap K_0$ at scales $2^{-j}$, $j\ge j_{0}$, with at most
$\lfloor2^{jd}\rfloor$ squares at each scale. By \eqref{fd:eq:Hj} and
\eqref{fd:eq:small-covers},
\[
 \lambda'_u(S)=\lambda'_u(S\cap K_0)
 \le\sum_{j\ge j_{0}}H_j(u)
 \le\sum_{j\ge j_{0}}j^{-2}.
\]
Letting $j_{0}\to\infty$ proves $\lambda'_u(S)=0$.
The set $Z_d$ was fixed before choosing $S$, so this conclusion holds
simultaneously for every such Borel set $S$.

We set
\[
 Z=\bigcup_{d\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,s)}Z_d.
\]
It is a Borel null set. For every $u\in I_0\setminus Z$ and every Borel
$S$ with $\dim_{\mathrm H} S<s$, we choose \(d\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,s)\) with
\(\dim_{\mathrm H} S<d<s\).
The preceding argument then gives
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:slice-result}
 \lambda'_u(S)=0.
\end{equation}
Thus, the claim holds for $\lambda'_u$ outside one Borel null set.

We now return to the rotations. Set $\theta=2\arctan u$. By
Lemma~\ref{fd:lem:cayley},
\begin{equation}\label{fd:eq:pushforward-chart}
 \lambda'_u=(\operatorname{Id}-u\mathsf J)_\#\lambda_{R_\theta}.
\end{equation}
The map $\operatorname{Id}-u\mathsf J$ is an invertible linear map of the plane.
It carries Borel sets to Borel sets and preserves Hausdorff dimension.
For every Borel set $S$,
\[
 \lambda_{R_\theta}(S)
 =\lambda'_u\bigl((\operatorname{Id}-u\mathsf J)S\bigr).
\]
Thus, \eqref{fd:eq:slice-result} implies that $\lambda_{R_\theta}$ gives
zero mass to every Borel set of dimension less than $s$ for almost all
\(\theta\in[-2\arctan(1/4),2\arctan(1/4)]\).
The exceptional angles form a null set because $d\theta/du$ is bounded
above and below on $I_0$.

Finitely many translated angle intervals cover all rotations. On an
interval centred at $\theta_0$, we have
\[
 R_\theta=R_{\theta-\theta_0}R_{\theta_0}.
\]
We apply the same argument to $(R_{\theta_0})_\#\mu$ and $\nu$.
Rotations preserve the support normalization and the Frostman bounds.
The finite union of the exceptional angle sets is null, so the claim
holds for almost all elements of $\mathrm{SO}(2)$.

We fix the reflection
$g_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Every orientation-reversing
$g\in\mathrm O(2)$ has the form $R_{\theta} g_0$. We apply the rotation result
to $(g_0)_\#\mu$ and $\nu$. Since Haar measure on $\mathrm O(2)$ gives each
component half its mass and is normalized angular measure on either
component, this proves Proposition~\ref{prop:full-dimension-measure} for
normalized supports.
A common dilation, as described before \eqref{fd:eq:normalization}, removes
that normalization. All exceptional sets constructed above are Borel,
so $\mathcal G$ may be chosen Borel. This completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
The measure statement is Proposition~\ref{prop:full-dimension-measure}.
For the set statement, we apply this proposition to Frostman measures
whose exponents approach the dimensions of $A$ and $B$.
We first treat the cases where one of these dimensions is zero.
If $\dim_{\mathrm H} A=0$, then for any $a\in A$ and every $g\in\mathrm O(2)$,
\[
 ga-B\subset gA-B,\qquad
 \dim_{\mathrm H}(ga-B)=\dim_{\mathrm H} B=\min\{\dim_{\mathrm H} A+\dim_{\mathrm H} B,2\}.
\]
If $\dim_{\mathrm H} B=0$, we use $gA-b\subset gA-B$ for any $b\in B$.
Thus, the claim holds for every $g$ in these cases.

Suppose that both dimensions are positive. We choose positive sequences
$\alpha_n\uparrow\dim_{\mathrm H} A$ and $\beta_n\uparrow\dim_{\mathrm H} B$, with
$\alpha_n<\dim_{\mathrm H} A$ and $\beta_n<\dim_{\mathrm H} B$.
By the compact form of Frostman's lemma, there are compact sets
$A_n\subset A$, $B_n\subset B$ supporting Frostman probabilities
$\mu_n,\nu_n$ with exponents $\alpha_n,\beta_n$, respectively.
Proposition~\ref{prop:full-dimension-measure} gives a Borel set
$\mathcal G_n\subset\mathrm O(2)$ of full measure for each pair.

Let $g\in\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathcal G_n$. The compact set $gA_n-B_n$
has mass one for $(g_\#\mu_n)*\widetilde\nu_n$, so the proposition gives
\[
 \dim_{\mathrm H}(gA-B)\ge\dim_{\mathrm H}(gA_n-B_n)
 \ge\min\{\alpha_n+\beta_n,2\}
 \quad\text{for every }n.
\]
Letting $n\to\infty$, we obtain
\[
 \dim_{\mathrm H}(gA-B)\ge\min\{\dim_{\mathrm H} A+\dim_{\mathrm H} B,2\}.
\]
The intersection of the sets $\mathcal G_n$ has full measure. In particular,
the endpoint $\dim_{\mathrm H} A+\dim_{\mathrm H} B=2$ is included, without a hypothesis on
the critical Hausdorff measures. This completes the proof.

label: lem:frostman-annular
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Bounded support extends the Frostman bound to radii greater than
one after multiplying its constant by a fixed factor.
We choose a nonnegative $\Phi_{\rm ann}\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ that is at least one on
$B(0,2)$. Fourier inversion, rapid decay of $\check\Phi_{\rm ann}$, and the
Frostman bound give

\begin{align*}
 \int_{|\xi|\le2R}|\widehat\omega(\xi)|^2\,d\xi
 &\le \int\Phi_{\rm ann}(\xi/R)|\widehat\omega(\xi)|^2\,d\xi\\
 &\lesssim R^2\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-jN}
   \int\omega(B(x,2^jR^{-1}))\,d\omega(x)
 \lesssim R^{2-t}\omega(\mathbb R^2),
\end{align*}

where $N>t$ is fixed. This proves \eqref{eq:frostman-annular}, and
polar coordinates give \eqref{eq:frostman-annular-polar}.
This completes the proof.

label: thm:WW
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:WW}
Let \(1<t<2\) and \(0<\beta_{\rm te}<\alpha_{\rm te}<1\). Suppose that the lines form a
Katz--Tao \((w,t)\)-set and that their \(w\)-ball shadings satisfy the
\((\alpha_{\rm te},\beta_{\rm te})\)-two-ends condition. Suppose also that each shading
has area at least \(c\lambda w\), for some \(\lambda>0\) and fixed \(c>0\),
and lies in a fixed bounded region.
Then, for every
\(\varepsilon>0\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:WW}
 \left|\bigcup_\ell Y(\ell)\right|
 \gtrsim
 w^{\varepsilon+t\alpha_{\rm te}/2}\lambda^{1/2}w^{(t-1)/2}
 \Gamma_{Y,2-t}^{-1/2}\sum_\ell |Y(\ell)|.
\end{equation}
The implicit constant may depend on \(\varepsilon,\alpha_{\rm te},\beta_{\rm te}\), the
two-ends constant, the Katz--Tao constant, and the fixed bounded region.
head: environment
name: Wang--Wu

label: rem:WW-conventions
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:WW-conventions}
The two-ends condition in \cite[Definition~1.2]{WW} is stated for
$w\times w^{\alpha_{\rm te}}$ tubes along a line. Our ball condition implies that
condition, since such a tube is covered by a fixed number of balls of
radius $w^{\alpha_{\rm te}}$. Conversely, the part of a ball of that radius within
a $w$-neighbourhood of a line is covered by a fixed number of those tubes.
Thus, the two formulations differ only in their constants.

We shall also use \eqref{eq:WW} for unions of $Cw$-balls, where $C\ge1$
is fixed and the other hypotheses are imposed on these shadings.
Here is the reduction. The Katz--Tao bound gives a fixed upper bound for
the number of line parameters within distance $2Cw$ of any one parameter.
A finite colouring therefore partitions the lines into $Cw$-separated
families. One family retains a fixed proportion of $\sum\limits_\ell|Y(\ell)|$.
On that family we apply the theorem at scale $\widetilde w=Cw$.
A ball of radius $\widetilde w^{\alpha_{\rm te}}$ is covered by a fixed number of balls of radius $w^{\alpha_{\rm te}}$, so the two-ends condition persists. Moreover,
\[
 \widetilde\lambda\sim\lambda,
 \qquad \Gamma_{Y,2-t}^{(\widetilde w)}
 \lesssim_C\Gamma_{Y,2-t}^{(w)},
\]
where the superscript indicates the scale used in the definition.
The latter bound follows directly by restricting the supremum to
$r\ge Cw$ and comparing the powers of the two scales. Substitution in
\eqref{eq:WW} proves the claimed version. A fixed dilation places the
ambient region in the unit ball used in \cite{WW}. It changes areas,
line-parameter distances and all radii by fixed factors; radii between
one and the original ambient diameter are handled by a fixed covering.
The same argument therefore proves the stated bounded-region version.

label: lem:KT-selection
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:KT-selection}
Fix $C_{\rm sep}\ge1$. Let $0<t\le2$ and let $\omega$ be a finite positive measure in a fixed bounded square with
$\omega(B(x,r))\le C_F r^t$, where $C_F>0$. Let $E$ be measurable
with $\omega(E)>0$, and let $0<w<1$. There is a finite
\(C_{\rm sep}w\)-separated set \(\mathcal {X}\subset E\) with
$|\mathcal X|\gtrsim\omega(E)/(C_Fw^t)$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:KT-selection}
 |\mathcal X\cap B(z,r)|\lesssim (r/w)^t
 \qquad(w\le r\le1).
\end{equation}
The constants may depend on $t$, the ambient square, and $C_{\rm sep}$, but
not on $C_F$, $E$, or $w$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Replacing \(w\) by a comparable dyadic length changes only the constants.
We shall select occupied squares subject to an upper bound in every
larger dyadic square. We use the measure to define a fractional flow,
then apply the integral max-flow theorem to obtain the selected squares.
Consider the finite dyadic tree from a fixed ambient square down to
squares of side \(w\), with edges directed away from the root. We give the edge
entering a square \(Q\) the capacity
\[
 b(Q)=\lfloor(\operatorname{side}(Q)/w)^t\rfloor.
\]
Let \(Q_0\) denote the root square. We join the source to \(Q_0\) by an
edge of capacity \(b(Q_0)\).
We join every terminal square meeting \(E\) in positive \(\omega\)-measure
to a sink by an edge of capacity one. If \(C\) is a sufficiently large
absolute constant, then
\[
 \frac{\omega(E\cap Q)}{CC_Fw^t}
 \le \tfrac12(\operatorname{side}(Q)/w)^t\le b(Q),
\]
and the left side is at most one for a terminal square. Additivity of
the measure makes these values a feasible flow of total value
\(\omega(E)/(CC_Fw^t)\). Since all capacities
are integers, the integral max-flow theorem \cite{FF} gives an integral flow of at
least this value. It therefore selects occupied terminal squares, at most
one from each terminal square and at most \(b(Q)\) below every dyadic
square \(Q\).

We choose one point of \(E\) in each selected terminal square. A ball of
radius \(r\ge w\) meets a bounded number of dyadic squares with side
between \(r\) and \(2r\), so the capacity bound gives
\eqref{eq:KT-selection}. Finally, we colour the terminal grid by the two
coordinate indices modulo a fixed integer larger than \(C_{\rm sep}+3\). A largest
colour class retains a fixed proportion of the points and has the required
separation. If \(\omega(E)/(C_Fw^t)<1\), the positive feasible flow still implies
that the integral maximum flow has value at least one, so the same argument
applies. This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: lem:dual
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:dual}
Let \(\omega\) be a compactly supported positive measure of mass at most one
with a \(t\)-Frostman upper bound, where
\(1<t<2\), and fix \(0<\beta_{\rm te}<\alpha_{\rm te}<1\).
In a fixed bounded slope chart, associate \(x=(x_1,x_2)\) with
\[
 \ell_x=\{(k,h_{\rm du}):h_{\rm du}=x_2-kx_1\}.
\]
Let \(x\mapsto D_x\) be a measurable family of unions of grid intervals
of length comparable to \(w\). For each nonempty \(D_x\), let
\(Y_x\) be the union of one \(Cw\)-ball centred on \(\ell_x\)
above each grid interval in \(D_x\). Suppose that these shadings satisfy the
\((\alpha_{\rm te},\beta_{\rm te})\)-two-ends
condition and lie in a measurable set \(S\). Then, for every
\(\varepsilon>0\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dual}
 \int|D_x|\,d\omega(x)
 \lesssim L_w
 w^{-(2\varepsilon+t\alpha_{\rm te})/(4-t)}|S|^{2/(4-t)}.
\end{equation}
The implicit constant may depend on the constants listed in
Theorem~\ref{thm:WW}, on the Frostman constant, and on the fixed charts,
but not on \(w\), \(S\), or the family \(D_x\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We group the points according to the lengths of their direction sets.
In each group, Lemma~\ref{lem:KT-selection} selects a Katz--Tao family
of dual lines. We then apply Theorem~\ref{thm:WW} to bound the measure
of that group in terms of $|S|$.

We divide the points for which \(D_x\ne\varnothing\) into \(O(L_w)\)
measurable classes
\[
 E_\lambda=\{x:\lambda\le |D_x|<2\lambda\},
 \qquad cw\le\lambda\le C,
\]
and consider a class with \(\omega(E_\lambda)>0\). We apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:KT-selection} to this class and denote the selected set by
\(\mathcal {X}\). The map
\(x\mapsto(-x_1,x_2)\), which gives the dual-line parameter, is an
isometry. The selected lines therefore form a Katz--Tao \((w,t)\)-set,
with
\[
 |\mathcal X|\gtrsim \omega(E_\lambda)w^{-t}.
\]
The separation constant in Lemma~\ref{lem:KT-selection} is chosen large
enough for the \(Cw\)-ball shadings. Bounded overlap along a line gives
\(|Y_x|\asymp\lambda w\). Moreover, for \(w\le r\le1\),
\[
 |Y_x\cap B(z,r)|\lesssim w\min\{r,\lambda\}.
\]
Hence,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gamma-lambda}
 \Gamma_{Y,2-t}\lesssim(\lambda/w)^{t-1}.
\end{equation}
To see this, the expression defining \(\Gamma_{Y,2-t}\) is at most
\[
 \begin{cases}
 C(r/w)^{t-1},&r\le\lambda,\\
 C(w/r)^{2-t}\lambda/w,&r\ge\lambda.
 \end{cases}
\]
Since \(\lambda\gtrsim w\), both bounds are
\(\lesssim(\lambda/w)^{t-1}\).

We apply Theorem~\ref{thm:WW} with the $Cw$-ball convention in
Remark~\ref{rem:WW-conventions}. Substituting \eqref{eq:gamma-lambda}
and the lower bound for $|\mathcal X|$ into \eqref{eq:WW} gives

\begin{align}
 |S|&\gtrsim
 w^{\varepsilon+t\alpha_{\rm te}/2}\lambda^{1/2}w^{(t-1)/2}
 (\lambda/w)^{-(t-1)/2}|\mathcal X|\lambda w\notag\\
 &\gtrsim w^{\varepsilon+t\alpha_{\rm te}/2}
 \omega(E_\lambda)\lambda^{(4-t)/2}.
 \label{eq:weighted-dual-key}
\end{align}

Raising both sides to the power $2/(4-t)$ and using
$\omega(E_\lambda)\le1$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \omega(E_\lambda)\lambda
 &\lesssim \omega(E_\lambda)^{(2-t)/(4-t)}
 w^{-(2\varepsilon+t\alpha_{\rm te})/(4-t)}|S|^{2/(4-t)}\\
 &\le w^{-(2\varepsilon+t\alpha_{\rm te})/(4-t)}|S|^{2/(4-t)}.
\end{align*}
Summing over the \(O(L_w)\) classes proves \eqref{eq:dual}.
This completes the proof.

label: lem:sector
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sector}
Let $\chi_I$ be as above, and let
$\phi$ be any fixed smooth annular cutoff.
Then, uniformly in $R\ge1$ and $I$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sector}
 \left\|\bigl[\phi(|\xi|/R)\chi_I(\xi/|\xi|)\bigr]^\vee\right\|_1
 \lesssim L_w.
\end{equation}
For two such cutoffs the corresponding product kernel has $L^1$ norm at
most $CL_w^2$. If an angular symbol is supported in an $O(w)$-arc and has
derivatives bounded by $C_kw^{-k}$, its annular kernel has uniformly
bounded $L^1$ norm.
The implicit constants may depend on the annular cutoff.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first rescale an arc of length $O(w)$ to obtain the uniform kernel
bound. For a longer arc, we estimate the two endpoint cutoffs separately.
Their kernels have a logarithmic $L^1$ bound.

By dilation, it suffices to take $R=1$. We may also assume that $w$
is sufficiently small; for $w$ bounded below the symbol has uniformly
bounded derivatives, and integration by parts gives the claim. First suppose that the angular
symbol is supported in an $O(w)$-arc. After a rotation, we rescale the second frequency coordinate by $w$.
The resulting symbol is supported in a fixed compact rectangle, with
the first frequency coordinate bounded away from zero, and all its derivatives are
bounded independently of $w$. Integration by parts and the change of
variables give a bounded $L^1$ norm for its inverse transform.

We prove the logarithmic bound by an explicit decomposition at the
endpoints. Divide the consecutive set $I$ into a fixed number of
consecutive blocks, each of angular length at most $\pi/8$. It suffices
to estimate one block. Blocks of length $O(w)$ were treated above. For
any other block $I'$, rotate its middle direction to angle zero.
The partition of unity shows that $\chi_{I'}$ is
one between its two endpoint regions and zero outside the block enlarged
by $O(w)$. Its derivative is supported in two disjoint intervals of
length $O(w)$, with endpoints $a,b\in[-\pi/8,\pi/8]$.
If $g_a$ and $g_b$ are the restrictions of
$\frac{d}{d\theta}\chi_{I'}(e_\theta)$ to these intervals, then
\[
 \int g_a=1,\qquad \int g_b=-1,
 \qquad
 \chi_{I'}(e_\theta)=\Psi_a(\theta)-\Psi_b(\theta),
\]
where
\[
 \Psi_a(\theta)=\int_{-\infty}^{\theta}g_a(v)\,dv,
 \qquad \Psi_b(\theta)=-\int_{-\infty}^{\theta}g_b(v)\,dv.
\]
Both steps are bounded, their derivatives of positive order are supported
within $O(w)$ of their endpoints, and
$|\Psi_a^{(k)}|+|\Psi_b^{(k)}|\le C_kw^{-k}$ for $k\ge1$.
Choose a fixed angular cutoff equal to one on $[-\pi/8,\pi/8]$ and
supported in $(-\pi/4,\pi/4)$. The support of the block lies in
$[-\pi/8,\pi/8]$ for sufficiently small $w$. Multiplication by this cutoff expresses
the block multiplier exactly as two localized endpoint multipliers.

For either endpoint, rotate it to angle zero. The angular cutoff and
the fixed annulus then give $c\le\xi_1\le C$. The step changes only
when $|\xi_2|\lesssim w$. Let $\Psi$ denote the endpoint function
$\Psi_a$ or $\Psi_b$ in the rotated coordinate. Differentiating
$\Psi(\arctan(\xi_2/\xi_1))$ shows, for every fixed $n\ge0$, that
the corresponding multiplier $\psi_{\rm end}$ satisfies
\[
 \|\partial_{\xi_1}^n\psi_{\rm end}\|_1\lesssim_n1,
 \qquad
 \|\partial_{\xi_1}^n\partial_{\xi_2}^k\psi_{\rm end}\|_1
 \lesssim_n w^{1-k}\quad(k=1,2).
\]
Each derivative in $\xi_1$ of the step supplies a factor $\xi_2/w$,
which is bounded on its transition region. Each derivative in $\xi_2$
costs $w^{-1}$ there,
and that region has area $O(w)$. Terms differentiated only on the fixed
cutoffs have bounded derivatives and support of bounded area.
Integration by parts in the two coordinates now gives
\[
 |\psi_{\rm end}^{\vee}(x_1,x_2)|
 \lesssim (1+|x_1|)^{-2}
 \min\{1,|x_2|^{-1},w^{-1}|x_2|^{-2}\}.
\]
The integral of the second factor is at most
\[
 2\left(1+\int_1^{1/w}\frac{dv}{v}
       +w^{-1}\int_{1/w}^{\infty}\frac{dv}{v^2}\right)
 \lesssim L_w.
\]
Summing the fixed number of pieces proves \eqref{eq:sector}.
For a product of two sector cutoffs, insert an additional smooth radial
cutoff equal to one on $\operatorname{supp}\phi$, factor the multiplier, and apply
the $L^1$ convolution inequality. This completes the proof.

label: thm:RD
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:RD}
For every $\varepsilon_{\rm dec}>0$, there is
$\delta_0(\varepsilon_{\rm dec})>0$ with the following property.
Let $R$ be sufficiently large, $r\in[R/2,2R]$, and
$0<\delta_{\rm freq}\le\delta_0(\varepsilon_{\rm dec})$.
Let $\mathcal W$ be a finite family of rectangular tubes in a fixed ball,
all of length one and of the same half-width
\[
 C_T R^{-1/2+\delta_{\rm freq}},
\]
where $C_T>0$ is fixed. In each fixed circle chart their directions
belong to a uniform angular lattice of mesh comparable to $r^{-1/2}$,
and tubes of each direction have
bounded overlap. For $T\in\mathcal W$, let $F_T$ be Schwartz with Fourier
support in a rectangular cap about the circle $\{\xi:|\xi|=r\}$, of tangential length
$O(R^{1/2})$ and normal thickness at most $r^{3\delta_{\rm freq}/4}$,
whose normal is parallel to $T$. Suppose that
\[
 \|F_T\|_{L^6(\mathbb R^2\setminus2.1T)}\le r^{-100}\|F_T\|_6,
 \qquad a\le\|F_T\|_6\le2a
\]
for some $a>0$ and every $T\in\mathcal W$.
Let $Y$ be a union of $r^{-1/2}$-squares in a fixed ball, and suppose
$1\le M\le|\mathcal W|$ and
\[
 |\{T\in\mathcal W:3T\cap60Q\ne\varnothing\}|\le M
 \quad\text{for every square }Q\subset Y.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:RD}
 \left\|\sum_{T\in\mathcal W}F_T\right\|_{L^6(Y)}^2
 \lesssim_{\varepsilon_{\rm dec},\delta_{\rm freq}}R^{\varepsilon_{\rm dec}}
 \left(\frac M{|\mathcal W|}\right)^{2/3}
 \sum_{T\in\mathcal W}\|F_T\|_6^2.
\end{equation}
The constant may also depend on $C_T$, the fixed balls, the circle charts
and the overlap bound.
head: environment
name: Refined decoupling

label: lem:light
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:light}
Let $1<t<2$, and let $\omega$ be a positive measure of mass at most one
in a fixed bounded ball, satisfying a $t$-Frostman upper bound.
Let $\mathrm l_j$ be selected using this same measure $\omega$ in
\eqref{eq:light-test}.
For every $\varepsilon_{\rm dec}>0$, when
$0<\delta_{\rm freq}\le\delta_0(\varepsilon_{\rm dec})$, $w=R^{-1/2+\delta_{\rm freq}}$, and $r\in[R/2,2R]$,

\begin{equation}\label{eq:light-operator}
 \left\|\sum_j \mathrm l_j(x)\int_{S^1}e^{2\pi irx\cdot e}f_j(e)\,d\sigma(e)\right\|_{L^2(\omega)}^2
 \lesssim_{\varepsilon_{\rm dec},\delta_{\rm freq}}R^{-t/3+\varepsilon_{\rm dec}}q^{2/3}
 \sum_j\|f_j\|_2^2
\end{equation}

for $f_j\in L^2(S^1)$ supported in $\operatorname{supp}\chi_j$.
The constant depends on the original Frostman constant. It is uniform
in the chosen patches and in subfamilies of angular cells.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We construct wave packets adapted to the selected strips and verify
the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:RD}. The strip-mass bound then
controls the smoothed measure on regions where many packets meet.
H\"older's inequality and refined decoupling cancel the multiplicity
factors and give \eqref{eq:light-operator}.

By homogeneity, we may normalize $\sum\limits_j\|f_j\|_2^2=1$.

After a fixed translation and dilation, we may assume that
\(\operatorname{supp}\omega\subset B(0,1/10)\); this changes only the implicit
constants.

We set \(\rho=r^{-1/2}\sim R^{-1/2}\). In the fixed circle charts
of Theorem~\ref{thm:RD}, we use a smooth partition into caps of angular
length \(O(\rho)\). Their centres belong to the lattices specified in
that theorem. Only a bounded number of the angular cells of length
\(O(w)\) meets any one of these finer caps.

On a fine cap centred at $e_\theta$, we use the parameter
$\theta+\rho u$, with $u$ in a bounded interval. We expand the input
in an orthonormal Fourier series on a slightly larger interval and
multiply by a fixed smooth function equal to one on the input support.
Let $c_{\theta,n}$ be the Fourier coefficients. We include
$c_{\theta,n}$ in the definition of the packet $\psi_{\theta,n}$, so the
contribution of the cap is $\sum\limits_n\psi_{\theta,n}$. These packets satisfy
\begin{align}
 \sum_{\theta,n}|c_{\theta,n}|^2&\lesssim1,\label{eq:coeff}\\
 |\psi_{\theta,n}(x)|
 &\lesssim_J |c_{\theta,n}|\rho^{1/2}
 \bigl(1+\operatorname{dist}(x,\ell_{\theta,n})/\rho\bigr)^{-J}
 \quad\text{for }x\in B(0,1),\label{eq:packet-point}\\
 \|\vartheta\psi_{\theta,n}\|_6^2
 &\lesssim \rho^{4/3}|c_{\theta,n}|^2
 \lesssim R^{-2/3}|c_{\theta,n}|^2.\label{eq:packet-six}
\end{align}
Here the parallel axes $\ell_{\theta,n}$ have spacing comparable to $\rho$
and direction $e_\theta$. The function $\vartheta$ is a fixed smooth cutoff
equal to one on $B(0,1/5)$ and supported in $B(0,1/2)$. To prove
\eqref{eq:packet-point}, we note that the phase after rescaling the cap has
the form
$n u+r\rho(x\cdot e_\theta^\perp)u+O(|x|u^2)$.
Its derivatives of order at least two are uniformly bounded. Integration
by parts gives the displayed transverse decay. Integrating its sixth power
over the support of $\vartheta$ gives \eqref{eq:packet-six}. Bounded chart
Jacobians and overlap affect only constants. These assertions hold for the
contribution of each coarse angular cell separately; the bounded overlap
gives \eqref{eq:coeff} for their combined collection.

We multiply each packet from coarse angular cell \(j\) by each \(\zeta_{j,k}\) for
which \((j,k)\) is chosen, and by \(\vartheta\). Since
\(|e_j-e_\theta|\lesssim w\), there are only \(O(1)\) transverse cutoffs
whose central lines lie within \(O(w)\) of \(\ell_{\theta,n}\) on
\(B(0,1/2)\). We retain these terms. For the other strip cutoffs,
\eqref{eq:packet-point} gives an error \(O(R^{-J})\) for any prescribed
\(J\), since \(w/\rho\sim R^{\delta_{\rm freq}}\). The same integration by parts allows us
to restrict to \(|n|\le R^2\), with error \(O(R^{-J})\) in supremum norm
for every prescribed \(J\).
In each error estimate below, we first fix the required power $J$
and then choose the integration-by-parts order sufficiently large.
This order may depend on $J/\delta_{\rm freq}$, but not on $R$.
There are at most \(CR^{5/2}\) remaining packets before
accounting for the bounded number of transverse cutoffs.

We also discard axes missing $B(0,3/4)$. On the support of
$\vartheta$, such an axis has a fixed positive separation, so
\eqref{eq:packet-point}, Cauchy--Schwarz in the coefficients, and summation
of the transverse tails give $O(R^{-J})$ for every prescribed $J$.
All remaining axes therefore meet the fixed ambient ball; their unit
segments and required dilations can be placed in $B(0,3)$.
Hence, the geometric containment hypothesis in Theorem~\ref{thm:RD} holds.

We associate each remaining product
$\vartheta\zeta_{j,k}\psi_{\theta,n}$ with a tube \(T\) about
\(\ell_{\theta,n}\) of length one and half-width \(C_{\rm pkt}w\),
centred at the point of the axis nearest the origin. The fine and coarse axes differ
by \(O(w)\) in the fixed ambient ball.
With these fixed choices, we have
\[
 3T\cap60Q\ne\varnothing
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 Q+B(0,cw)\subset C_*G_{j,k},
\]
where \(c\) is the fixed enlargement needed for smoothing at scale
\(R^{-1}\). These choices are independent of the measure and the scale.
Every tube comes from a chosen index \((j,k)\), so the strip on the
right satisfies \eqref{eq:light-test}.


For a fixed fine direction, the axes initially have spacing $\rho$. We
split their indices modulo a sufficiently large fixed multiple of
$w/\rho\sim R^{\delta_{\rm freq}}$. The tubes of half-width $C_{\rm pkt}w$ then have bounded overlap within
each residue class. A further bounded colouring separates the $O(1)$
coarse angular cells and strip cutoffs. All resulting families meet the directional
and overlap conditions in \eqref{eq:RD}.

We next verify the Fourier support and decay required in
Theorem~\ref{thm:RD}. Before inserting
the spatial cutoffs, each packet is supported on its fine circle cap in
Fourier space. The transverse cutoff $\zeta_{j,k}$ has Fourier frequencies
along $e_j^\perp$. We truncate these frequencies at $R^{\delta_{\rm freq}/4}/w$.
Their component normal to the fine cap is
$O(w)R^{\delta_{\rm freq}/4}/w=O(R^{\delta_{\rm freq}/4})$, and their tangential component is
$O(R^{1/2-3\delta_{\rm freq}/4})$. We likewise truncate the Fourier transform of
$\vartheta$ at $R^{\delta_{\rm freq}/4}$. The discarded parts, and their needed
derivatives, are $O(R^{-J})|c_{\theta,n}|$ for every prescribed $J$, since
the original cutoffs are smooth.

If \(L_\zeta=R^{\delta_{\rm freq}/4}/w\), the curvature of the circle contributes the
additional normal error
\[
 O(L_\zeta r^{-1/2}+L_\zeta^2/r)
 =O(R^{-3\delta_{\rm freq}/4}+R^{-3\delta_{\rm freq}/2}),
\]
which is smaller than the allowed normal thickness.


For each tube \(T\), let \(P_T\) be a smooth Fourier multiplier equal to
one on the truncated support. Its support is a rectangle of tangential
length $O(R^{1/2})$ and normal thickness at most $r^{3\delta_{\rm freq}/4}/10$.
After rescaling the two coordinates, its kernel has uniformly bounded
$L^1$ norm. We define
\[
 F_T=P_T\bigl(\vartheta\zeta_{j,k}\psi_{\theta,n}\bigr).
\]
The function inside the multiplier is smooth and compactly supported,
so $F_T$ is Schwartz. By definition, it has the exact Fourier support
required in \eqref{eq:RD}, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:packet-six-sum}
 \sum_T\|F_T\|_6^2\lesssim R^{-2/3}.
\end{equation}
After summing all $O(R^{5/2})$ projected packets, the projection and
truncation errors on \(\operatorname{supp}\omega\) are still $O(R^{-J})$ in supremum
norm, upon increasing the integration-by-parts orders. The projection kernel has
rapid decay outside transverse distance $O(\rho)$ and longitudinal distance
$O(R^{-3\delta_{\rm freq}/4})$. Together with \eqref{eq:packet-point}, this gives an
absolute $L^6$ tail $O(R^{-J})|c_{\theta,n}|$ outside $2.1T$. There is a
fixed transverse margin: the strip cutoff is supported in a smaller
transverse dilation of \(T\), while \eqref{eq:packet-point} controls the
spatial tails of the original wave packet. In the longitudinal direction,
$\operatorname{supp}\vartheta\subset B(0,1/2)$ lies a fixed positive distance from
the ends of $2.1T$, by our choice of the centre of $T$.
Thus, after summing over the charts,

\begin{equation}\label{eq:packet-decomposition-error}
 \vartheta\sum_j \mathrm l_jE_rf_j=\sum_TF_T+\mathcal E_J,
 \qquad
 \|\mathcal E_J\|_{L^\infty(\operatorname{supp}\omega)}\lesssim_J R^{-J},
\end{equation}

provided the integration-by-parts orders are sufficiently large.

We discard the packets with \(\|F_T\|_6<R^{-100}\). Their Fourier
supports lie in \(B(0,CR)\), so Bernstein's inequality gives
\(\|F_T\|_\infty\lesssim R^{1/3}\|F_T\|_6\). We choose the projection and
tail errors above to be \(O(R^{-400})|c_{\theta,n}|\).

Since \(\sum\limits_{\theta,n}|c_{\theta,n}|^2\lesssim1\), we have
\(|c_{\theta,n}|\lesssim1\). For the retained packets,
\[
 \frac{\|F_T\|_{L^6(\mathbb R^2\setminus2.1T)}}{\|F_T\|_6}
 \lesssim R^{-300}\le r^{-100}
\]
for sufficiently large $R$. This is the relative decay required in
Theorem~\ref{thm:RD}.

The packet count
and Bernstein's inequality show that the discarded contribution is
\(O(R^{-50})\) on \(\operatorname{supp}\omega\); the implicit constant may depend on
\(\delta_{\rm freq}\). By \eqref{eq:packet-six-sum},
\(\|F_T\|_6\lesssim1\). We divide the remaining packets into
\(O(\log R)\) classes in which the \(L^6\) norms lie in one
interval \([2^k,2^{k+1})\). Thus, they differ by at most a factor of two. Each class now
satisfies the Fourier support and decay hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{thm:RD}.

We now estimate the mass of the smoothed measure where tubes overlap.
We fix one of these classes, in one chart and one residue class, and
denote its family of tubes by $\mathcal W$. Let $F=\sum\limits_{T\in\mathcal W}F_{T}$.
The reproducing
inequality used in \eqref{eq:trace} gives
\[
 \|F\|_{L^2(\omega)}^2\lesssim\int|F(x)|^2v_R(x)\,d x,
 \qquad v_R=\omega*\Phi_R,
 \quad \|v_R\|_\infty\lesssim R^{2-t},\quad\|v_R\|_1\lesssim1.
\]
Outside the fixed ambient ball, the $L^{3/2}$ norm of $v_R$ is
$O(R^{-J})$ for every fixed $J$, while $\|F\|_6$ has a polynomial bound
by \eqref{eq:packet-six-sum} and the packet count. H\"older's inequality
therefore bounds this contribution by $O(R^{-50})$. We tile that ball by
$\rho$-squares and write
\[
 n(Q)=|\{T:3T\cap60Q\ne\varnothing\}|.
\]
We group the squares according to the dyadic ranges
$M\le n(Q)<2M$ and denote their union by $Y_M$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:RD} applies to $Y_M$ with multiplicity parameter
$\min\{2M,|\mathcal W|\}$, which changes its bound by at most a fixed factor.
The containment proved above, together with the strip bound, gives

\begin{equation}\label{eq:multiplicity-mass}
 \int_{Y_M}v_R\lesssim\frac{|\mathcal W|q}{M}
 +O\!\left(\frac{|\mathcal W|}{M}R^{-J}\right).
\end{equation}

For every square in $Y_M$, the count $n(Q)$ is at least $M$. Hence,
\[
 M\int_{Y_{M}}v_{R}
 \le\sum_{T}\sum_{\substack{Q\subset Y_M\\3T\cap60Q\ne\varnothing}}
        \int_{Q}v_{R}.
\]
For each tube, the union of these squares and its fixed
$w$-neighbourhood lie in $C_*G_{j,k}$. Smoothing at scale
$R^{-1}\ll w$ bounds the corresponding integral by $Cq+O(R^{-J})$,
using \eqref{eq:light-test}. Thus, the last sum is at most
$C|\mathcal W|q+O(|\mathcal W|R^{-J})$, which proves \eqref{eq:multiplicity-mass}.
Since $|\mathcal W|\lesssim R^{5/2}$ and $M\ge1$, we can make its error
$O(R^{-200})$ by increasing $J$.

H\"older's inequality, \eqref{eq:RD}, and \eqref{eq:multiplicity-mass} now give

\begin{align*}
 \int_{Y_M}|F|^2v_R
 &\le \|F\|_{L^6(Y_M)}^2
        \|v_R\|_\infty^{1/3}\left(\int_{Y_M}v_R\right)^{2/3}\\
 &\lesssim R^{\varepsilon_{\rm aux}}R^{(2-t)/3}
     \left(\frac M{|\mathcal W|}\right)^{2/3}
     \left(\frac{|\mathcal W|q}{M}\right)^{2/3}
     \sum_T\|F_T\|_6^2+O(R^{-50})\\
 &\lesssim R^{\varepsilon_{\rm aux}+(2-t)/3}q^{2/3}
     \sum_T\|F_T\|_6^2+O(R^{-50}).
\end{align*}

Squares with \(n(Q)=0\) lie outside every $2.1T$, so the decay estimate controls their contribution. The sum over the $O(\log R)$ values of $M$ costs a logarithmic factor. The charts, residue classes, and packet-norm ranges partition the packets into at most $R^{C\delta_{\rm freq}}(\log R)^C$ families. We apply Cauchy--Schwarz to their sum and use \eqref{eq:packet-six-sum} for the total packet energy. Together with \eqref{eq:packet-decomposition-error}, this gives
\[
 \left\|\sum_{j} \mathrm l_{j}E_{r}f_{j}\right\|_{L^2(\omega)}^2
 \lesssim R^{-t/3+\varepsilon_{\rm aux}+C\delta_{\rm freq}}(\log R)^Cq^{2/3}+O(R^{-50}).
\]
We first choose \(\varepsilon_{\rm aux}<\varepsilon_{\rm dec}/4\), and then decrease $\delta_0(\varepsilon_{\rm dec})$ so that the packet estimate \eqref{eq:RD} holds with loss $\varepsilon_{\rm aux}$ and \(C\delta_0(\varepsilon_{\rm dec})<\varepsilon_{\rm dec}/4\). The argument holds
for every \(0<\delta_{\rm freq}\le\delta_0(\varepsilon_{\rm dec})\). The remaining power of $R^{\varepsilon_{\rm dec}}$
absorbs the fixed logarithmic factors. Since $q\ge w$ and $1<t<2$,
the error $O(R^{-50})$ is absorbed as well. This proves
\eqref{eq:light-operator}. The proof is unchanged for a subfamily of
coarse angular cells. This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: imp:terminal
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{imp:terminal}
The construction terminates after finitely many rounds, all final
coefficients are measurable, and for every $n,j,k$,
\[
 k\in\mathcal P_{n,j}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a_{jk}>h_n.
\]
In each slope chart, every final set $D_{n,x}$ satisfies the
 two-ends condition at scale $w^{\alpha_c}$ with exponent $\beta_c$.
 Its fixed $O(w)$ thickening, and the associated $Cw$-ball shading
 in the dual plane, satisfy the corresponding condition with exponent
 $\beta_c/2$ for sufficiently small $w$. Here $C$ is any fixed
 enlargement constant.
At each $x$, the final selected set $\{j:c_j(x)=1\}$ is the union of at most
\[
 K\lesssim w^{-\beta_c}L_w^2
\]
recorded intervals of length $O(w^{\alpha_c})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first verify termination and identify the final bin lists.
We then count the recorded intervals and check the two-ends condition.
There are finitely many entries $(n,j,k)$ in the lists. Each round
either ends the construction or removes an entry. Thus, the construction
terminates. The operation at each point is finite and
measurable as explained above, and every residual mass is an integral
of a measurable function.

The masses $a_{jk}$ decrease throughout. If a bin is absent from a list
at any stage, its mass at that stage is at most the corresponding
threshold. Its final mass is no larger. Conversely, the final test
removes every bin whose mass is at most its threshold. This proves the
stated equivalence.

For a fixed $x$, chart, and threshold $n$, the set $D_{n,x}$ only
shrinks during the entire construction. Each angular interval
recorded because of that threshold deletes more than a
$C_{\rm 2e}^{-1}w^{\beta_c}$ fraction of its current length.
Other angular deletions and bin updates can only reduce this length.
The initial length is bounded, and any nonempty set of cells has
length at least a fixed multiple of $w$. Thus, the number of such
records is at most
\[
 1+\frac{\log(C/w)}{-\log(1-C_{\rm 2e}^{-1}w^{\beta_c})}
 \lesssim w^{-\beta_c}L_w.
\]
There are $O(L_w)$ thresholds and a fixed number of charts,
giving the asserted bound on $K$.

At the final round every set defined by the lists passes the angular
test, and the lists do not change thereafter. Thus, all the final sets
satisfy the two-ends condition.
For a fixed $O(w)$ thickening, the cells contributing to its
intersection with an interval of length $O(w^{\alpha_c})$ lie in an
$O(w)$ enlargement of that interval. Within the chart, this enlargement
is covered by a bounded number of the test intervals. Each original
cell contributes only a bounded number of neighboring cells. Thus,
the final tests bound the thickened intersection by $Cw^{\beta_c}$
times the original total length, and hence by the same factor times
the thickened total length. The passage to areas of ball shadings
changes only fixed constants. For sufficiently small $w$, these
constants are absorbed by replacing $\beta_c$ with $\beta_c/2$.
This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: imp:terminal-tail
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We estimate the area occupied by the dual rectangles in terms of
$M(q)$. The two-ends estimate then gives an inequality for $M(q)$.
We first take $q=h_n$ and fix one slope chart. Let $M_{\rm ch}(h_n)$
be its contribution to $M(h_n)$. The occupied dual rectangles have
area at most
\[
 Cw^2|\{(j,k):j\text{ belongs to the chart},\ a_{jk}>h_n\}|
 \le C\frac{w}{h_n}M_{\rm ch}(h_n).
\]
To see this, let $s_j$ be the central slope. Up to a fixed sign,
$x\cdot e_j^\perp=(x_2-s_jx_1)/\sqrt{1+(s_j)^2}$, so a transverse bin
fixes the dual height at $s_j$ to an interval of length $O(w)$.
Varying the slope across $J_j$ changes the height by at most
$O(w)|x_1|=O(w)$. One fixed enlargement therefore contains the
$Cw$-ball shading associated with each occupied bin.
By Lemma~\ref{imp:terminal}, these shadings satisfy the two-ends
condition. Lemma~\ref{lem:dual} gives
\[
 M_{\rm ch}(h_n)\lesssim L_w
 w^{-(2\varepsilon_F+t\alpha_c)/(4-t)}
 \left(\frac{w}{h_n}M_{\rm ch}(h_n)\right)^{2/(4-t)}.
\]
If $M_{\rm ch}(h_n)>0$, we divide by its power on the right and raise
to $(4-t)/(2-t)$. This gives
\[
 M_{\rm ch}(h_n)\lesssim
 L_w^{(4-t)/(2-t)}w^{-(2\varepsilon_F+t\alpha_c)/(2-t)}
 (h_n/w)^{-p_t}.
\]
The estimate is immediate when $M_{\rm ch}(h_n)=0$. We sum over the
fixed number of charts. For an intermediate $q$, we choose the largest
$h_n\le q$. Then $q<2h_n$, and monotonicity gives the same bound.
This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: imp:cap-bin-energy
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{imp:cap-bin-energy}
Let $\tau$ be a positive measure supported in the fixed ambient ball,
and set $a_k=\tau(Q_{jk})$. Uniformly for $r\sim R$,
\[
 \int_{S^1}|\chi_j(e)\widehat\tau(re)|^2\,d\sigma(e)
       \lesssim w\sum_k a_k^2.
\]
No spatial regularity of a density defining $\tau$ is required.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Expanding the square gives
\[
 \int_{S^1}|\chi_j(e)\widehat\tau(re)|^2\,d\sigma(e)
 =\iint K_{j}(x-y)\,d\tau(x)\,d\tau(y),
\]
where
\[
 K_j(x-y)=\int_{S^1}|\chi_j(e)|^2
                     e^{-2\pi i r(x-y)\cdot e}\,d\sigma(e).
\]
Bounded support and repeated angular integration by parts give
\[
 |K_j(z)|\lesssim_N
 w(1+|z\cdot e_j^\perp|/w)^{-N}.
\]
For transverse separation $O(w)$, the bound follows from the length
of the cap. Outside a sufficiently large fixed multiple of $w$, the phase
derivative is comparable to $R|z\cdot e_j^\perp|$. Smoothness of the
cap and $Rw^2\geq1$ give the displayed decay.
For $x\in Q_{jk}$ and $y\in Q_{j,k'}$ this is bounded by
$C_Nw(1+|k-k'|)^{-N}$. Thus, the left side is at most
\[
 C_N w\sum_{k,k'}(1+|k-k'|)^{-N}a_k a_{k'}
 \lesssim w\sum_k a_k^2,
\]
by the $\ell^2$ convolution inequality for a summable sequence.
This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: imp:fixed-source-bounds
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: imp:positive-source-light
title: Proof
body_md:
We first apply the light estimate to one fixed positive restriction
of $\omega$. We then partition the selected angular sets into dyadic
intervals, so that this estimate applies to each resulting restriction.
Let $I$ be an angular interval made up of cells, and let
$\omega_0\le\omega$ be a fixed positive measure. Suppose that, for
$j\in I$, each strip selected in $\mathrm l_j$ has enlarged-strip
$\omega_0$-mass at most $(4C_*+2)h$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:light}
to these cells with $q=(4C_*+2)h$, which lies in $[w,1]$ for
sufficiently large $R$. The Frostman constant is unchanged.
To apply duality, define
\[
 \mathcal E_{\rm sel}f(x)=\sum_{j\in I}\mathrm l_j(x)
    \int_{S^1}e^{2\pi irx\cdot e}\chi_j(e)f(e)\,d\sigma(e).
\]
The lemma and bounded angular overlap give
\[
 \|\mathcal E_{\rm sel}\|_{L^2(\sigma)\to L^2(\omega_0)}^2
 \lesssim R^{-t/3+\varepsilon_{\rm dec}}h^{2/3}.
\]
Here we used $\sum\limits_j\|\chi_jf\|_2^2\lesssim\|f\|_2^2$.
Fubini's theorem identifies the adjoint as
\[
 \mathcal E_{\rm sel}^*F(e)=\sum_{j\in I}\chi_j(e)
       \int e^{-2\pi irx\cdot e}\mathrm l_j(x)F(x)\,d\omega_0(x).
\]
Thus, $\|\mathcal E_{\rm sel}^*1\|_2^2\le\|\mathcal E_{\rm sel}\|^2
\|1\|_{L^2(\omega_0)}^2$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{imp:positive-source-light}
 \left\|\sum_{j\in I}\chi_j(e)\int e^{-2\pi irx\cdot e}
                  \mathrm l_j(x)\,d\omega_0(x)\right\|_{L^2(\sigma)}^2
 \lesssim R^{-t/3+\varepsilon_{\rm dec}}h^{2/3}\omega_0(\mathbb R^2).
\end{equation}
No spatial regularity of the density defining $\omega_0$ is needed.

At each point $x$, we cut the cyclic angular grid at a fixed index and
partition the consecutive blocks with $c_j(x)=0$ into canonical dyadic
intervals. At any given length there are at most $2(K+1)$ such intervals.
For each dyadic interval $I$, let $\xi_I(x)$ indicate that this interval
is selected, and set $\omega_I=\xi_I\omega$. The choices are measurable,
and the partition gives
\[
 1-c_{j}(x)=\sum_{I:j\in I}\xi_I(x).
\]
Therefore,
\[
 \mathcal F_{\omega}^{\mathrm l}(re)
 =\sum_{I}\sum_{j\in I}\chi_j(e)
   \int e^{-2\pi irx\cdot e}\mathrm l_{j}(x)\,d\omega_{I}(x).
\]
For $j\in I$, we have $\omega_I\le\omega_j$. Thus, each patch in
$\mathrm l_j$ has enlarged-strip $\omega_I$-mass at most $(4C_*+2)h$.
Apply \eqref{imp:positive-source-light} to the cells $j\in I$ with
this one fixed measure. The squared norm of their contribution is at most
$CR^{-t/3+\varepsilon_{\rm dec}}h^{2/3}\omega_I(\mathbb R^2)$.

At one dyadic length the angular supports have bounded overlap, and
\[
 \sum_{I\text{ of this length}}\omega_I(\mathbb R^2)\le2(K+1).
\]
There are $O(L_w)$ lengths. Cauchy--Schwarz across these lengths gives
\[
 S_\omega^{\mathrm l}(r)\lesssim
 (K+1)L_w^2R^{-t/3+\varepsilon_{\rm dec}}h^{2/3}.
\]
Since $K+1\lesssim w^{-\beta_c}L_w^2$, this proves
\eqref{imp:light}.

For $c$, we decompose the blocks with $c_j(x)=1$ in the same way.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:frostman-annular}, each resulting positive restriction
has annular energy bounded by $CR^{2-t}$ times its mass.
Bounded overlap at each length
and Cauchy--Schwarz across lengths give
\[
 \int_{R/2}^{2R}rS_\omega^c(r)\,d r
 \lesssim (K+1)L_w^2R^{2-t}.
\]
For $b=1$, Lemma~\ref{lem:frostman-annular} gives the estimate
without this factor. Substituting the bound for $K+1$ proves
\eqref{imp:ann}.
This completes the proof.

label: imp:cluster-pair
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix source points $x,y$. For a pair of their angular intervals $I,J$,
the product of the corresponding cutoffs after a random
rotation is identically zero unless their smooth supports meet. This
occurs with probability at most $C(|I|+|J|+w)$, whereas the nonzero
annular kernel has $L^1$ norm at most $CL_w^2$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:sector}. Thus, the integral in $g$ of the $L^1$ norm
of the kernel for this pair is at most
$CL_w^2(|I|+|J|+w)$. Summing gives
\[
 CL_w^2\left(K_\nu\sum_I|I|+K_\mu\sum_J|J|
                      +K_\mu K_\nu w\right)
 \le CL_w^2(K_\nu\Lambda_\mu+K_\mu\Lambda_\nu+K_\mu K_\nu w).
\]
Integration over the probability measures in $x,y$, and translation
invariance of the kernel norm, prove \eqref{imp:cluster-general}.
For positive finite measures the right side is multiplied by
the product of their masses. The same argument works on each
component of $\mathrm O(2)$.

For the clustered symbols, the selected cells form at most $K$ disjoint
consecutive blocks of total length at most $CKw^{\alpha_c}$, by
Lemma~\ref{imp:terminal}. Applying the common-bound estimate and
using $w\le w^{\alpha_c}$ gives \eqref{imp:cc}.
This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: imp:layer
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We count the bins supporting one layer and use their upper mass bound
to estimate its circular energy. Minkowski's inequality then allows
us to sum over the layers.
A newly selected patch has an enlargement meeting a bin of mass $>q$
but none of mass $>2q$. Every bin in its support is within boundedly many
bin indices of such a bin. There are at most $M(q)/(wq)$ bins of mass $>q$,
and each has boundedly many neighbors. The enlarged strip contains
each support bin, giving its upper mass bound.
By bounded angular overlap and Lemma~\ref{imp:cap-bin-energy},
\begin{align*}
 \int_{S^1}\left|\sum_j\chi_j(e)\widehat\tau_j(re)\right|^2\,d\sigma(e)
 &\lesssim\sum_{j}\int_{S^{1}}
       |\chi_{j}(e)\widehat\tau_{j}(re)|^{2}\,d\sigma(e)\\
 &\lesssim w\sum_{j,k}\tau_j(Q_{jk})^2.
\end{align*}
This proves \eqref{imp:schur}. Applying it to
$\tau_j=b_{q,j}\omega$, we obtain
\[
 S_{\omega}^{b_{q}}(r)\lesssim w\frac{M(q)}{wq}(Cq)^2
 \lesssim qM(q).
\]
Lemma~\ref{imp:terminal-tail} proves \eqref{imp:layer-bound}.
The identity $d=\sum\limits_{n=0}^{n_h-1}b_{2^nh}$ and Minkowski's inequality
then give
\begin{align*}
 S_\omega^d(r)^{1/2}
 &\le\sum_{n=0}^{n_h-1}S_\omega^{b_{2^nh}}(r)^{1/2}\\
 &\lesssim
 L_w^{(4-t)/(2(2-t))}w^{-(2\varepsilon_F+t\alpha_c)/(2(2-t))}
 A_{\rm d}(h)^{1/2}\sum_{n\ge0}2^{n(1-p_t)/2}.
\end{align*}
The series converges because $p_t>1$, and
$A_{\rm d}(h)=h(h/w)^{-p_t}=wH^{1-p_t}$.
Squaring proves \eqref{imp:base-residual}. The constants have the
same dependencies as in Lemma~\ref{imp:terminal-tail}.
This completes the proof.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We choose the parameters so that the clustered pair has summable
$L^1$ norms and the other pairs have summable $L^2$ norms.
On a fixed ball, these bounds give an $L^1$ density for $\lambda_g$.
By decreasing the Frostman exponent, we may assume that
$s_0<t<4/3$. A common dilation and separate translations place
both supports in the fixed ball used above. These operations change
each rotated difference measure only by a dilation and a translation,
so they preserve absolute continuity.

We first choose all parameters independently of $R$.
If we first set $w=R^{-1/2}$ and omit the auxiliary losses, the two
quantities to be summed are
\begin{equation}\label{imp:decay-exponents}
 R^{2-t}A_{\rm l}(h)=w^{(8t-10-2b_0)/3},\qquad
 R^{2-t}A_{\rm d}(h)=w^{2t-3+(p_t-1)b_0}.
\end{equation}
Both powers are positive precisely when
\begin{equation}\label{imp:threshold-choice}
 \frac{(3-2t)(2-t)}{t}<b_0<4t-5,
\end{equation}
since $p_t-1=t/(2-t)$. The difference between the upper and lower
endpoints is
\[
 (4t-5)-\frac{(3-2t)(2-t)}{t}
 =\frac{2(t^2+t-3)}{t}>0.
\]
Thus, $t>s_0$ makes this interval nonempty. Its endpoints lie
between $0$ and $1$ because $s_0<t<4/3$.
We make the following choices in order.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Choose $b_0$ satisfying \eqref{imp:threshold-choice}, and let
\[
 \Delta=\min\left\{\frac{4t-5-b_0}{3},
        \frac{2t-3+(p_t-1)b_0}{2}\right\}>0.
\]
These are the two decay exponents in $R$ before the auxiliary losses.
\item Fix the analytic loss and the angular parameters by
\[
 \varepsilon_{\rm dec}=\frac{\Delta}{16},\qquad
 \alpha_c=\min\left\{\frac14,
                  \frac{\Delta(2-t)}{64(1+t)}\right\},\qquad
 \beta_c=\frac{\alpha_c}{4},\qquad
 \varepsilon_F=\frac{\alpha_c}{2}.
\]
In particular, $0<2\beta_c<\alpha_c<1$ and
\[
 \beta_c\le\frac{\Delta}{256},\qquad
 \frac{2\varepsilon_F+t\alpha_c}{2-t}\le\frac{\Delta}{64}.
\]
\item Let $\delta_0(\varepsilon_{\rm dec})$ be supplied by
Lemma~\ref{lem:light}, and choose
\[
 0<\delta_{\rm freq}<
 \min\left\{\delta_0(\varepsilon_{\rm dec}),\frac14,
 \frac{\Delta}{16\left(1+(p_t-1)b_0+\frac23(1-b_0)\right)}\right\}.
\]
Use $w=R^{-1/2+\delta_{\rm freq}}$ and the definitions in
\eqref{imp:scale-parameters} at every dyadic scale $R$.
\end{enumerate}
All constants below may depend on these fixed choices and on the
original Frostman constants, but not on $R$.

The norms below are taken over $dm(g)\,dz$.
Plancherel's theorem, polar coordinates and invariance of Haar
measure give
\begin{equation}\label{imp:rotation-identity}
 \|T_R(b_1,b_2)\|_2^2
 =2\pi\int_0^\infty r|\phi(r/R)|^2
                 S_\mu^{b_1}(r)S_\nu^{b_2}(r)\,dr.
\end{equation}
Here the first and second symbols use $\mu$ and $\nu$, respectively.
The identity $c+\mathrm l+d=1$ implies
\[
 1-c_\mu c_\nu
 =\mathrm l_\mu+d_\mu+c_\mu\mathrm l_\nu+c_\mu d_\nu.
\]
Hence,
\[
 P_R\lambda_g=B_R(g,\cdot)+G_R(g,\cdot),
\]
where
\begin{align*}
 B_R&=T_R(c,c),\\
 G_R&=T_R(\mathrm l,1)+T_R(d,1)+T_R(c,\mathrm l)+T_R(c,d).
\end{align*}
In every term of $G_R$, one factor is $\mathrm l$ or $d$ and has a
circular estimate; the other is $1$ or $c$ and has an annular
estimate. Equations \eqref{imp:light}, \eqref{imp:ann},
\eqref{imp:base-residual}, and \eqref{imp:rotation-identity} therefore
show that
\begin{equation}\label{imp:output-bounds}
 \begin{split}
 \|B_R\|_1&\lesssim w^{\alpha_c-2\beta_c}L_w^6,\\
 \|G_R\|_2^2&\lesssim R^{2-t}\left[
 R^{\varepsilon_{\rm dec}}w^{-2\beta_c}L_w^8A_{\rm l}(h)
 +w^{-\beta_c-(2\varepsilon_F+t\alpha_c)/(2-t)}
 L_w^{(4-t)/(2-t)+4}A_{\rm d}(h)\right].
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
The first estimate is \eqref{imp:cc}.

For completeness, the two terms in the second estimate, with their
logarithms omitted, are $R^{-e_{\rm light}}$ and
$R^{-e_{\rm heavy}}$, where
\begin{align*}
 e_{\rm light}
 &=\frac{4t-5-b_0}{3}
   -\frac{2\delta_{\rm freq}}3(1-b_0)
   -\varepsilon_{\rm dec}-(1-2\delta_{\rm freq})\beta_c,\\
 e_{\rm heavy}
 &=\frac{2t-3+(p_t-1)b_0}{2}
   -\delta_{\rm freq}\bigl(1+(p_t-1)b_0\bigr)
   -\left(\frac12-\delta_{\rm freq}\right)
       \left(\beta_c+\frac{2\varepsilon_F+t\alpha_c}{2-t}\right).
\end{align*}
Our choices give $e_{\rm light},e_{\rm heavy}\ge3\Delta/4$.
For example, the loss in the first line is at most
$\Delta/16+\Delta/16+\Delta/256<\Delta/4$; that in the
second is at most
$\Delta/16+(\Delta/256+\Delta/64)/2<\Delta/4$.
The fixed logarithmic powers are at most $R^{\Delta/4}$ for large $R$.
Also, $\alpha_c-2\beta_c=\alpha_c/2$ and
$1/2-\delta_{\rm freq}>1/4$. Hence, after absorbing $L_w^6$,
\begin{equation}\label{imp:base-decay}
 \|B_R\|_1\lesssim R^{-\alpha_c/16},\qquad
 \|G_R\|_2^2\lesssim R^{-\Delta/2}.
\end{equation}
Thus, both estimates decay with fixed positive powers of $R$.

The measures $\lambda_g=(g_\#\mu)*\widetilde\nu$ are supported in
one fixed ball. Let $V$ be a larger ball whose boundary has positive
distance from that ball. The Schwartz kernel of the fixed annular
multiplier gives
\[
 \|P_R\lambda_g\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^2\setminus V)}=O_N(R^{-N}),
\]
uniformly in $g$, for every $N>0$. On $V$, the decomposition
and Cauchy--Schwarz give
\begin{equation}\label{imp:annular-L1-decay}
 \int_{\mathrm O(2)}\|P_R\lambda_g\|_1\,dm(g)
 \le\|B_R\|_1+|V|^{1/2}\|G_R\|_2+O_N(R^{-N})
 \lesssim R^{-\zeta_{\rm dec}}
\end{equation}
for some $\zeta_{{\rm dec}}>0$. This argument requires no support condition on
$B_R$ or $G_R$.

The right side of \eqref{imp:annular-L1-decay} is summable over
dyadic $R$. By Tonelli's theorem,
\[
 \sum_R\|P_R\lambda_g\|_{1}<\infty
\]
for almost all $g$. Hence, $\sum\limits_RP_R\lambda_g$ converges in $L^1$ for these $g$. The low-frequency part in \eqref{eq:dyadic-resolution} is also in $L^1$, since it is the
convolution of a finite measure with a Schwartz function. The
resolution of the identity identifies the resulting sum with
$\lambda_g$ as a distribution. Hence, $\lambda_g$ has an $L^1$
density for almost all $g$. The rotation identity holds on both
components of $\mathrm O(2)$.

For Borel sets $A,B$, we choose
\[
 s_0<t<\min\{4/3,\dim_{\mathrm H} A,\dim_{\mathrm H} B\}.
\]
Frostman's lemma gives $t$-Frostman probabilities on compact subsets
of $A$ and $B$. For almost all $g$, their convolution is an
absolutely continuous probability supported on a compact subset
of $gA-B$. Thus, $\mathcal L^2(gA-B)>0$. The difference set is analytic
and hence Lebesgue measurable. This completes the proof.

label: imp:integrability
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{imp:integrability}
Under the measure hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{thm:breaking-four-thirds}, there is $\eta_{\rm int}>0$ such that
the densities $f_g=d\lambda_g/d\mathcal L^2$ satisfy
\[
 \int_{\mathrm O(2)}\int_{\mathbb R^2}f_g(z)^{1+\eta_{\rm int}}\,dz\,dm(g)<\infty.
\]
If $A',B'$ are compact sets supporting these probabilities, then
\[
 \int_{\mathrm O(2)}\mathcal L^2(gA'-B')^{-\eta_{\rm int}}\,dm(g)<\infty.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We interpolate the averaged $L^1$ estimate with the $L^\infty$
bound supplied by the Frostman condition. H\"older's inequality
will then give the assertion about the difference sets.
Let $t\in(s_0,4/3)$ be the exponent chosen in the preceding proof.
Since $\nu$ is a probability, the Frostman bound for $\mu$ gives
\[
 \lambda_{g}(B(z,r))
 =\int\mu\bigl(B(g^{-1}(z+y),r)\bigr)\,d\nu(y)
 \le C_{\mu} r^{t}
\]
for $g\in\mathrm O(2),z\in\mathbb R^{2},0<r\le1$.
The annular Schwartz kernel then gives
\[
 \|P_R\lambda_{g}\|_{L^\infty(dm(g)\,dz)}\lesssim R^{2-t}.
\]
Interpolating this with \eqref{imp:annular-L1-decay} yields
\[
 \|P_R\lambda_{g}\|_{L^{1+\eta_{\rm int}}(dm(g)\,dz)}
 \lesssim R^{[-\zeta_{\rm dec}+(2-t)\eta_{\rm int}]/(1+\eta_{\rm int})}.
\]
We choose $0<\eta_{\rm int}<\zeta_{\rm dec}/(2-t)$. Then the dyadic series
converges in $L^{1+\eta_{\rm int}}(dm(g)\,dz)$, and its sum, including the smooth
low-frequency term, is the density already identified in $L^1$.
This proves the first claim.

For almost all $g$, H\"older's inequality on $gA'-B'$ gives
\[
 1\le\mathcal L^2(gA'-B')^{\eta_{\rm int}/(1+\eta_{\rm int})}\|f_g\|_{1+\eta_{\rm int}}.
\]
Raising to the power $1+\eta_{\rm int}$, we obtain
\[
 \mathcal L^2(gA'-B')^{-\eta_{\rm int}}
 \le\|f_g\|_{1+\eta_{\rm int}}^{1+\eta_{\rm int}}
 =\int_{\mathbb R^{2}}f_{g}(z)^{1+\eta_{\rm int}}\,dz.
\]
The second claim follows by integration in $g$. This completes the proof.
